shots.text: He made his bricks twice as thick, because the tax man counted bricks.
In seventeen eighty-four, Britain needed money to pay for its war in America.
Parliament put a tax on every single brick, two shillings and sixpence per thousand.
Officers walked into the brickyards and counted the wet bricks, row by row, before firing.
And the price kept climbing, to four shillings per thousand by seventeen ninety-four.
But the law only counted bricks. It never said how big a brick could be.
You see, it's like paying for pizza by the slice. Cut bigger slices, and you pay for fewer.
In Measham, brickmaker Joseph Wilkes made bricks about twice as thick as normal.
They became known as Wilkes' gobs, and a wall needed far fewer of them.
Then the government struck back. Any brick bigger than ten by five by three inches paid double.
So brickmakers shrank their moulds again, and the giant bricks stopped.
The tax lasted until eighteen fifty. But some of Wilkes' giant bricks are still standing today.
